title: Debounce is a sliding window: algorithms for frontend engineers
description: You already ship algorithms, even if you've never called them that. These 50 questions connect five of them to code you write every day: stable sorting and locale-aware collation in data tables, sliding windows and two pointers in debounce, throttle, and infinite scroll, memoization that grows into dynamic programming (from `useMemo` to overlapping subproblems), edit distance and fuzzy matching in "did you mean…?" and fuzzy finders, and the greedy, backtracking, and line-breaking algorithms inside CSS. Every answer has been checked and links to MDN, Wikipedia, or a primary source so you can verify it yourself.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: What makes a sorting algorithm **stable**?

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: The same table re-sorted by Date. A stable sort keeps the Name order within each date; an unstable sort scrambles it.

options.text: Equal elements keep their original order after sorting.
It runs in the same time no matter how the input is arranged.
It never throws, even with a malformed comparator.
Sorting the same array twice returns the exact same array reference.

questions.explanation: A stable sort keeps elements that compare equal in their input order. If two rows tie on the sort key, the one that came first stays first. Stability is only about ties; it says nothing about speed or error handling. In UI tables it matters all the time, because ties should keep whatever order the user already had. Since ES2019, `Array.prototype.sort` is guaranteed to be stable.

questions.title: A user sorts a table by **Name**, then clicks the **Date** header. Why do rows with the same date stay in name order only if the sort is **stable**?
questions.description: Most data grids build multi-column sorting this way: sort by one column, then re-sort by another.

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: Sort by Name, then stably by Date, and you get "by Date, then by Name" for free.

options.text: A stable sort keeps the existing Name order among rows with the same Date, so the second sort layers on top of the first.
A stable sort is faster, so the second sort finishes before the rows repaint.
Only a stable sort can read two fields (Name and Date) in a single pass.
Stability guarantees the Date column is parsed before the Name column.

questions.explanation: To sort by several keys, sort by the *least* important key first, then stably sort by the more important ones. After sorting by Name, a stable sort by Date keeps same-date rows in Name order, so you get "by Date, then by Name" without writing a compound comparator. An unstable sort would scramble the Name order within each date. That's why frontend tables need stability.

questions.title: What's the bug in `array.sort((a, b) => a < b)`?
questions.description:
```js
array.sort((a, b) => a < b); // comparator returns true/false, not a number
```

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: The note at the bottom: a comparator must return a number, and `a < b` returns a boolean.

options.text: A comparator must return a *number*. `a < b` returns a boolean, which is never negative, so the array stays effectively unsorted.
It sorts in descending order instead of ascending.
It mutates `a` and `b`, corrupting the original objects.
It works for numbers but throws a `TypeError` for strings.

questions.explanation: `sort` expects the comparator to return a *negative* number (a goes first), `0` (equal), or a *positive* number (b goes first). A boolean is coerced to a number, `true` to `1` and `false` to `0`, so this comparator only ever returns `1` or `0`. It **never** returns the negative value that says "a goes first". In V8 the engine concludes everything is already in order: `[3, 1, 2, 10, 5].sort((a, b) => a < b)` comes back unchanged, while `(a, b) => a - b` gives `[1, 2, 3, 5, 10]`. Always return a number.

questions.title: Why does `[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort()` produce `[1, 10, 2, 20, 3]` instead of numeric order?

options.text: With no comparator, `sort` converts each element to a string and compares UTF-16 code units, so `"10"` sorts before `"2"`.
`sort` rounds each number to one significant digit before comparing.
`sort` is unstable for numbers, so the order is random.
`sort` orders by digit count first, then by value.

questions.explanation: Without a comparator, `sort` turns every element into a string and compares the strings code unit by code unit. For `"10"` and `"2"`, the first characters decide: `"1"` (code unit 49) is less than `"2"` (50), so `"10"` comes first. The numeric values never come into it. This is the most common `sort` surprise in JavaScript. For numbers, pass a comparator: `[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

questions.title: French users report that `"éclair"` sorts *after* `"zebra"` in your list. What's the right fix?

options.text: Use a locale-aware comparator such as `a.localeCompare(b, 'fr')` or a reused `Intl.Collator` instead of the default code-unit order.
Uppercase every string before calling the default `sort`.
Strip accents so `"é"` becomes `"e"`, then use the default `sort`.
Set the page's `lang` attribute to `fr` so `sort` picks up the locale automatically.

questions.explanation: The default sort compares UTF-16 code units. `"é"` is U+00E9 (233), which is *greater* than every unaccented ASCII letter, including `"z"` (122), so accented words get pushed to the end of the list. *Collation* is the set of language rules that puts `"é"` next to `"e"`, where readers expect it. Use `localeCompare`, or one reused `Intl.Collator` when sorting many items. Stripping accents loses information, and it's still wrong for languages where accented letters sort as separate letters.

questions.title: Since ES2019, `Array.prototype.sort` is guaranteed stable. What exactly does the spec require?

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: ES2019 requires a stable result, not a particular algorithm.

options.text: Only that the *result* is stable. Engines can use any algorithm they like (V8 uses TimSort).
Every engine must implement merge sort specifically.
Sorting must complete in O(*n*) time.
The array must be sorted in place with no auxiliary memory.

questions.explanation: The spec requires a *property*, that equal elements keep their order, and leaves the *implementation* to each engine. V8 switched to TimSort (a stable, adaptive merge sort) in Chrome 70, replacing an unstable quicksort for larger arrays. So "stable" is a contract you can rely on, while the algorithm, its complexity, and its memory use are engine details.

questions.title: Which statements about stable sorting and comparators are true?

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: A stable second pass keeps the order the first pass set up.

options.text: To sort by a primary key and then a secondary key with a stable sort, sort by the *secondary* key first.
A comparator that returns `0` declares the two elements equal, and a stable sort keeps their input order.
`arr.sort()` sorts in place and returns the *same* array, while `[...arr].sort()` leaves the original untouched.
A stable sort guarantees O(*n* log *n*) worst-case time.
Returning `a - b` from a comparator only works when `a` and `b` are strings.

questions.explanation: Layered sorting works because the last stable pass, on the primary key, keeps the order that earlier passes set up. So you sort by the *least* important key first. A comparator that returns `0` means "equal", and stability breaks the tie by input order. `sort` mutates the array and returns it, so copy first (`[...arr]` or `arr.slice()`) if you need the original. The two false claims: stability says nothing about time complexity, and `a - b` is the comparator for *numbers* (subtracting non-numeric strings gives `NaN`).

questions.title: Which of these comparators correctly sort an array of numbers in **ascending** order?

images.alt: Three columns showing the same four rows. The first, sorted by Name, reads Ana Mar 3, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Dee Mar 1. The second, re-sorted by Date with a stable sort, reads Bo Mar 1, Dee Mar 1, Ana Mar 3, Cy Mar 3, keeping name order inside each date. The third, re-sorted with an unstable sort, reads Dee Mar 1, Bo Mar 1, Cy Mar 3, Ana Mar 3, with the ties scrambled. A footer says ES2019 requires the stability property, not a specific algorithm, and that V8 uses TimSort. A highlighted note says a comparator must return a negative, zero, or positive number, and that a comparator written as a less-than test returns a boolean, which becomes 0 or 1 and so can never say "a first".
images.caption: For ascending order, the comparator returns a negative number when `a` should come first.

options.text: `(a, b) => Math.sign(a - b)`

questions.explanation: For ascending order, the comparator must return a *negative* number when `a` should come first. `a - b` does that. The ternary returns `-1`, `0`, or `1`, and `Math.sign(a - b)` reduces the difference to the same three values, so all three work. `b - a` sorts *descending*. `a < b` is the classic bug: it returns a boolean that becomes `0` or `1`, never negative, so the array stays effectively unsorted.

questions.title: Which `Intl.Collator` and `localeCompare` behaviors are real and useful for ordering UI lists?

options.text: `{ numeric: true }` makes `"file2"` sort before `"file10"` instead of after it.
`{ sensitivity: 'base' }` treats `"a"`, `"á"`, and `"A"` as equal for comparison.
Reusing one `Intl.Collator` is faster than calling `localeCompare` in a tight loop.
`{ numeric: true }` converts non-numeric strings to `NaN` and drops them from the result.
`localeCompare` returns `true` or `false`, like the `<` operator.

questions.explanation: With `numeric: true`, embedded numbers compare by value, so `"1" < "2" < "10"`. That's the fix for natural ordering of file names and version numbers. With `sensitivity: 'base'`, only base letters count, so `"a"`, `"á"`, and `"A"` compare equal, which is handy for accent- and case-insensitive matching. Creating one `Intl.Collator` and reusing its `.compare` avoids loading locale data on every call, a real saving in large sorts. The false options: `numeric` doesn't drop non-numeric strings, and `localeCompare` returns a negative, zero, or positive *number*, not a boolean.

questions.title: Type the value at index `1` (the second element) of `[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort()`.
questions.description: No comparator is passed, so the default string comparison applies.
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, `sort()` compares the *string* forms by code unit and returns `[1, 10, 2, 20, 3]`. So index `1` holds **10**, not `2`: `"10"` sorts right after `"1"` because they share the leading `"1"`. Anyone who forgets `(a, b) => a - b` runs into this sooner or later.

questions.title: What's the core difference between **debounce** and **throttle**?

images.alt: Three timelines over the same 1,200 milliseconds, each with ten event ticks: a fast burst of seven, a pause, then three more. The first lane shows every event, all ten. The second, debounce with a 200 millisecond wait, has two filled marks, each landing after a burst goes quiet. The third, throttle at 150 milliseconds, has four filled marks spread through the bursts. Two panels below list where each one fits. Debounce: search-as-you-type, autosave, validating a field after typing stops, and settled window resizes. Throttle: scroll position, mousemove and drag updates, infinite-scroll checks, and analytics pings.
images.caption: Same events, two clocks: debounce waits for a pause, throttle fires at a steady rate.

options.text: Debounce waits for events to stop for a quiet period, then fires once. Throttle fires at most once per fixed interval while events keep coming.
Debounce fires on every event; throttle fires only on the very first event.
Debounce is for scroll and throttle is for keyboard; otherwise they're identical.
Throttle waits for activity to stop; debounce caps the rate.

questions.explanation: Both limit how often a handler runs, but they use different clocks. **Debounce** resets a timer on every call and fires only after the calls *pause* for the chosen delay, like an elevator door that closes once people stop walking in. **Throttle** runs the handler right away, then ignores further calls until a fixed interval has passed, which gives a steady maximum rate during continuous activity. The option "Throttle waits for activity to stop; debounce caps the rate" swaps the two definitions, a common slip in interviews.

questions.title: A two-pointer or sliding-window scan replaces a brute-force nested loop. What does that usually do to the time complexity?

images.alt: Four snapshots of the string a b c a b c b b with a window drawn over it. At right = 2 the window covers abc, length 3. At right = 3 the incoming a repeats, so left jumps past index 0 and the window becomes bca, length 3. At right = 5 the window is abc again, length 3. At right = 6 the incoming b repeats, so left jumps past index 4 and the window shrinks to length 2. The longest window is 3. Two panels note that left and right only ever move forward, so every index enters and leaves once, 2n moves in total, while testing every substring would cost O(n squared) windows times O(n) to check each. They also list which problems suit a window.
images.caption: `left` and `right` only move forward, so every index enters and leaves the window once.

options.text: It turns an O(*n*²) double loop into a single O(*n*) pass, because both indices only move forward.
It turns O(*n*) into O(log *n*) by halving the window on each step.
It leaves complexity unchanged and only reduces memory use.
It turns O(*n*) into O(*n*²) because two indices must be tracked.

questions.explanation: Two pointers are fast because they only move one way. A `left` and a `right` index sweep across the data, and neither ever moves back. Each one advances at most *n* times, so the total work is O(*n*) even as the window grows and shrinks. Re-scanning every subarray from scratch would cost O(*n*²). This isn't binary search, which needs sorted data and gives O(log *n*) lookups. The technique fits whenever you can update the answer for one window to get the answer for the next.

questions.title: A **fixed-window** rate limiter (say, 100 requests per clock minute) has a well-known flaw that a **sliding-window** limiter fixes. What is it?

options.text: A client can send 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00, about 200 in two seconds across the window boundary.
Fixed windows leak memory because their counters are never reset.
Fixed windows must sort every request by timestamp, making them O(*n* log *n*).
Fixed windows physically cannot count more than one request per second.

questions.explanation: A fixed window resets its counter at hard boundaries, once per clock minute. A client can send requests at the very end of one window and the very start of the next, briefly doubling the intended rate around the boundary. A *sliding window* counts requests over the last N seconds from *now*, so there's no boundary to exploit and no burst at the edge. It's the same idea as the algorithmic sliding window, applied to traffic over time.

questions.title: What behavior does a **token-bucket** limiter allow that a strict, perfectly even rate does not?

options.text: Short bursts: unused capacity builds up as tokens, so a client that was quiet can briefly exceed the steady rate.
It guarantees exactly even spacing between every single request.
It blocks all requests until the bucket is completely full.
It removes the need for any limit by queuing requests forever.

questions.explanation: A token bucket refills at a steady rate up to a maximum, and each request spends a token. Unused tokens pile up (up to the cap), so a client that has been idle can spend its saved balance in a quick burst. Once the bucket is empty, the client drops back to the refill rate. It allows bursts while still capping the long-run average, which is why it's popular for APIs and for UI actions that arrive in clumps.

questions.title: In a virtualized list, what's the point of **overscan**, rendering a few extra rows just outside the viewport?

options.text: Rows just outside the visible window are already rendered, so fast scrolling doesn't flash blank gaps while new rows mount.
It doubles each row's height to reduce the total number of rows.
It caches every row that has ever been visible, growing without bound.
It switches virtualization off after the user scrolls past the first screen.

questions.explanation: List virtualization renders only the rows in a *window* around the viewport instead of all *n* rows, which keeps the DOM small: O(visible rows) instead of O(*n*). *Overscan* widens that window by a few rows on each side. When the user scrolls fast, the next rows are already mounted, so there's no flash of empty space while React commits new nodes. You do a little extra rendering in exchange for smoother scrolling. Overscan doesn't cache rows forever, and it doesn't change row heights.

questions.title: Which scenario is the textbook fit for **debounce** rather than throttle?

images.alt: Three timelines over the same 1,200 milliseconds, each with ten event ticks: a fast burst of seven, a pause, then three more. The first lane shows every event, all ten. The second, debounce with a 200 millisecond wait, has two filled marks, each landing after a burst goes quiet. The third, throttle at 150 milliseconds, has four filled marks spread through the bursts. Two panels below list where each one fits. Debounce: search-as-you-type, autosave, validating a field after typing stops, and settled window resizes. Throttle: scroll position, mousemove and drag updates, infinite-scroll checks, and analytics pings.
images.caption: Search-as-you-type sits in the debounce column.

options.text: Firing a search request only after the user stops typing in the search box.
Keeping a scroll-position progress bar updating smoothly as the user scrolls.
Sampling pointer coordinates at a steady rate during a drag.
Sending an analytics heartbeat every 5 seconds while a video plays.

questions.explanation: Search-as-you-type is the classic debounce case. You only care about the *final* query once the user pauses, so you reset the timer on each keystroke and send one request when typing stops, instead of one per character. The other three need a *steady* rhythm during continuous activity. That's throttle's job (often via `requestAnimationFrame` for scroll), or a plain fixed interval for the heartbeat.

questions.title: Which statements about windowing techniques in the browser are true?

images.alt: Three timelines over the same 1,200 milliseconds, each with ten event ticks: a fast burst of seven, a pause, then three more. The first lane shows every event, all ten. The second, debounce with a 200 millisecond wait, has two filled marks, each landing after a burst goes quiet. The third, throttle at 150 milliseconds, has four filled marks spread through the bursts. Two panels below list where each one fits. Debounce: search-as-you-type, autosave, validating a field after typing stops, and settled window resizes. Throttle: scroll position, mousemove and drag updates, infinite-scroll checks, and analytics pings.
images.caption: Debounce fires after a burst ends; throttle keeps firing during it.

options.text: Throttling a `scroll` handler with `requestAnimationFrame` limits the work to about one run per frame.
Debounce suits resize-driven layout recalculation that only needs the *final* size.
A sliding window over a stream keeps a running aggregate (count, sum, max) as it advances.
Throttle and debounce both guarantee the callback eventually runs for *every* event.
Virtualization renders all rows but hides the off-screen ones with `display: none`.

questions.explanation: Tying a scroll handler to `requestAnimationFrame` throttles it to the display's refresh rate, often 60 runs a second. Debounce fits resize recalculation because the in-between sizes don't matter; you want the size after the user stops dragging. A sliding window updates its running total as it moves, so each step is O(1). The false claims: debounce and throttle both *drop* events on purpose, and virtualization never mounts off-screen rows at all, which is the whole point.

questions.title: Which tasks are better served by **throttle** than by debounce?

images.alt: Three timelines over the same 1,200 milliseconds, each with ten event ticks: a fast burst of seven, a pause, then three more. The first lane shows every event, all ten. The second, debounce with a 200 millisecond wait, has two filled marks, each landing after a burst goes quiet. The third, throttle at 150 milliseconds, has four filled marks spread through the bursts. Two panels below list where each one fits. Debounce: search-as-you-type, autosave, validating a field after typing stops, and settled window resizes. Throttle: scroll position, mousemove and drag updates, infinite-scroll checks, and analytics pings.
images.caption: Throttle keeps firing while the activity continues; debounce waits for it to end.

options.text: Updating a reading-progress bar continuously as the user scrolls.
Repositioning a tooltip that follows the cursor during `mousemove`.
Firing infinite-scroll loads at most once per 300 ms while the user keeps scrolling.
Sending a search request only after the user finishes typing.
Auto-saving a draft only once the user pauses editing for 2 seconds.

questions.explanation: Throttle is the right choice when you want *regular updates during* continuous activity. A progress bar, a tooltip that follows the cursor, and rate-capped infinite-scroll loads all need to keep responding while the gesture continues, just not on every single event. The other two care only about the *end* of the activity (search after typing, save after a pause), and that's what debounce is for. A quick test: do you want updates *while* it happens (throttle), or one update *after* it settles (debounce)?

questions.title: Which problems can a **sliding-window** or **two-pointer** approach solve in a single O(*n*) pass?

images.alt: Four snapshots of the string a b c a b c b b with a window drawn over it. At right = 2 the window covers abc, length 3. At right = 3 the incoming a repeats, so left jumps past index 0 and the window becomes bca, length 3. At right = 5 the window is abc again, length 3. At right = 6 the incoming b repeats, so left jumps past index 4 and the window shrinks to length 2. The longest window is 3. Two panels note that left and right only ever move forward, so every index enters and leaves once, 2n moves in total, while testing every substring would cost O(n squared) windows times O(n) to check each. They also list which problems suit a window.
images.caption: A window over a contiguous range, updated step by step as it slides.

options.text: Length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
Maximum sum of any `k` consecutive elements.
Smallest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least a target (all numbers positive).
Whether *any* two elements anywhere in an *unsorted* array sum to a target.
Sorting the array into ascending order.

questions.explanation: Sliding windows work best on questions about *contiguous ranges*, where moving the window updates the answer step by step. For the longest substring without repeats, grow on the right and shrink from the left when you hit a duplicate. For the max sum of `k` in a row, slide a fixed-size window. For the smallest subarray with a sum ≥ target, shrinking from the left is safe only because all the values are positive. The two wrong options don't fit the pattern. Finding any pair that sums to a target in an *unsorted* array needs a hash set (the two-pointer version needs sorted input), and sorting is an O(*n* log *n*) problem, not a window scan.

questions.title: With a sliding window, what's the length of the longest substring of `"abcabcbb"` with no repeating characters?
questions.description: The window grows to take in new characters and shrinks from the left when a character repeats.

images.alt: Four snapshots of the string a b c a b c b b with a window drawn over it. At right = 2 the window covers abc, length 3. At right = 3 the incoming a repeats, so left jumps past index 0 and the window becomes bca, length 3. At right = 5 the window is abc again, length 3. At right = 6 the incoming b repeats, so left jumps past index 4 and the window shrinks to length 2. The longest window is 3. Two panels note that left and right only ever move forward, so every index enters and leaves once, 2n moves in total, while testing every substring would cost O(n squared) windows times O(n) to check each. They also list which problems suit a window.
images.caption: The window over `"abcabcbb"` never grows past 3.

questions.explanation: Grow the window to the right. Whenever the incoming character is already in the window, move `left` past its previous position. For `"abcabcbb"`, the best windows are `"abc"`, `"bca"`, and `"cab"`, so the answer is **3**. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so the scan is O(*n*), compared with O(*n*²) or O(*n*³) for checking every substring. It's the classic sliding-window interview problem.

questions.title: `useMemo`, `React.memo`, and reselect selectors all use the same classic technique. Which one?

options.text: They are all **memoization**: cache a result keyed by its inputs and reuse it while those inputs are unchanged.
They are all **lazy evaluation**: the value is never computed until it is first painted.
They are all **currying**: they split a function into one-argument steps.
They are all **debouncing**: they delay the computation until inputs settle.

questions.explanation: Each one stores a computed value and returns it again as long as its inputs haven't changed. `useMemo` caches a value across renders, `React.memo` skips re-rendering a component whose props haven't changed, and reselect caches derived state. That's *memoization*: spending memory to save time by remembering input→output pairs. Once you see the shared idea, the React APIs you use every day connect to the algorithm underneath.

questions.title: Which two properties does a problem need for **dynamic programming** to be the right tool?

images.alt: The full call tree for a naive recursive fib(5): fifteen nodes over five levels, branching into fib(4) and fib(3) and down to fib(1) and fib(0) leaves. Six nodes compute their value for the first time; the other nine are shaded as repeats of work done elsewhere in the tree. A side note says fib(40) takes over 300 million calls. Two panels below compare two approaches. Top-down memoization adds a cache so each distinct n is computed once, but keeps the recursion stack. Bottom-up tabulation fills the same table left to right with no recursion, shown as the climbing-stairs table where n = 1 through 5 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
images.caption: Nine of the fifteen calls in `fib(5)` repeat work already done: overlapping subproblems.

options.text: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
Constant time and constant space.
A sorted input and a balanced tree.
Tail recursion and immutable data.

questions.explanation: Dynamic programming pays off when a problem has two properties. *Overlapping subproblems*: the same smaller problems come up again and again, so caching their answers avoids exponential recomputation. *Optimal substructure*: the best overall solution is built from the best solutions to those subproblems. Memoization relies on the first property, and the recurrence relies on the second. Without overlap, caching gains nothing; without optimal substructure, combining sub-answers doesn't give a correct result.

questions.title: What distinguishes **top-down memoization** from **bottom-up tabulation**?

images.alt: The full call tree for a naive recursive fib(5): fifteen nodes over five levels, branching into fib(4) and fib(3) and down to fib(1) and fib(0) leaves. Six nodes compute their value for the first time; the other nine are shaded as repeats of work done elsewhere in the tree. A side note says fib(40) takes over 300 million calls. Two panels below compare two approaches. Top-down memoization adds a cache so each distinct n is computed once, but keeps the recursion stack. Bottom-up tabulation fills the same table left to right with no recursion, shown as the climbing-stairs table where n = 1 through 5 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
images.caption: One recurrence, two routes: top-down with a cache, or bottom-up with a table.

options.text: Top-down recurses from the goal and caches results as it goes; bottom-up loops up from the base cases and fills a table.
Top-down is always asymptotically faster than bottom-up.
Bottom-up can only handle problems with a single base case.
Top-down never uses extra memory, while bottom-up always does.

questions.explanation: Both solve the same recurrence. *Top-down* (memoization) writes the natural recursion starting from the target and stores each subproblem's answer the first time it's computed, so repeats are O(1) lookups. *Bottom-up* (tabulation) starts from the base cases and fills a table in a loop until it reaches the target, with no recursion. For the same recurrence, both have the same time complexity. They differ in call-stack use, in which subproblems get computed, and in how easily you can shrink the table.

questions.title: When can wrapping a value in `useMemo` make a component **slower**?

options.text: When the computation is cheap and the dependencies change on most renders, so you pay for a cache that almost never hits.
When the component never re-renders at all.
Whenever the dependency array has more than three entries.
Only when the app is running in development mode.

questions.explanation: Memoization is a trade. You spend memory, plus the work of storing the value and comparing the dependency array, to avoid recomputing. If the computation is cheap (a small `map` or some arithmetic) and the dependencies change every render, the cache rarely hits. You keep paying for the bookkeeping, never collect the savings, and the code gets noisier too. Algorithm textbooks rarely cover this frontend lesson: memoizing cheap work that's invalidated often can hurt.

questions.title: Why does this `useMemo` recompute on **every** render?

options.text: An object or array literal in the dependency array is a new reference on every render, so the dependencies never compare equal.
`useMemo` ignores object dependencies entirely.
Objects in a dependency array are compared by deep value, which always differs.
`useMemo` accepts only one dependency, so the extras are dropped.

questions.explanation: React compares dependencies with `Object.is`, which checks objects by reference. The literal `{ dir: 'asc' }` creates a new object on every render, so it never equals the previous one and the memo is invalidated every time. You pay for the computation *and* the caching. To fix it, move the constant outside the component, keep it in state or a ref, or list only primitive values (`[rows, dir]`). This reference-equality trap is the most common reason a memo "does nothing".

questions.title: Naive recursive `fib(n)` (two recursive calls, no cache) takes exponential time. What does memoization bring it down to?

images.alt: The full call tree for a naive recursive fib(5): fifteen nodes over five levels, branching into fib(4) and fib(3) and down to fib(1) and fib(0) leaves. Six nodes compute their value for the first time; the other nine are shaded as repeats of work done elsewhere in the tree. A side note says fib(40) takes over 300 million calls. Two panels below compare two approaches. Top-down memoization adds a cache so each distinct n is computed once, but keeps the recursion stack. Bottom-up tabulation fills the same table left to right with no recursion, shown as the climbing-stairs table where n = 1 through 5 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
images.caption: Naive `fib(5)` makes 15 calls, and 9 of them repeat work.

options.text: O(*n*) time, because each of the *n* distinct subproblems is computed once and reused.
O(log *n*), because the recursion tree becomes balanced.
O(*n*²), because each cache lookup is linear.
Still exponential, because memoization saves only memory, not time.

questions.explanation: Naive `fib` recomputes the same values over and over: `fib(5)` calls `fib(3)` twice and `fib(2)` three times, and the waste grows to roughly O(2^*n*). Those repeats are *overlapping subproblems*. With memoization, each distinct value from `fib(0)` to `fib(n)` is computed once and then read from the cache in O(1), so the whole thing takes O(*n*) time and O(*n*) space. The exponential tree collapses into a line. It's the standard example of why caching subproblems matters.

questions.title: Which statements about memoization and dynamic programming are true?

options.text: Memoization trades memory for time by storing previously computed results.
Memoization is only correct for **pure** functions, whose output depends only on their arguments.
Bottom-up tabulation can sometimes cut memory to O(1) by keeping only the last few rows.
Any recursive function can be memoized safely for a speedup, even one with random output.
Optimal substructure means the input must already be sorted.

questions.explanation: Memoization spends memory to avoid recomputation, and it's only valid for *pure* functions. If the same arguments can give different results (randomness, the current time, outside mutation), a cache hit returns a stale or wrong value. Tabulation often needs only the last one or two rows of its table; for Fibonacci, keeping just the last two values brings space down to O(1). The false claims: memoizing an impure or random function is unsafe, and *optimal substructure* is about combining optimal sub-answers, not about sorted input.

questions.title: What makes a **correct** memoization cache key?

options.text: It captures every input the result actually depends on.
Equal inputs always produce equal keys (for example, a stable serialization of the arguments).
An impure input like the current time must be part of the key, or the cached value will be wrong.
It can skip some arguments to save space, as long as the function is fast.
A mutable object used by reference is always a safe key across renders.

questions.explanation: A cache key has to *identify the computation*. It must include everything the output depends on, and equal inputs must map to equal keys, so the serialization has to be normalized (for example, not dependent on property order). If a value like `Date.now()` affects the result, leaving it out of the key gives stale hits. The false options are real bugs. Dropping a relevant argument lets different inputs share one key and return wrong results. A mutable object keyed by reference can be changed in place: the reference stays the same, the contents change, and the cache silently returns a stale value.

questions.title: Which trade-offs between top-down memoization and bottom-up tabulation are real?

images.alt: The full call tree for a naive recursive fib(5): fifteen nodes over five levels, branching into fib(4) and fib(3) and down to fib(1) and fib(0) leaves. Six nodes compute their value for the first time; the other nine are shaded as repeats of work done elsewhere in the tree. A side note says fib(40) takes over 300 million calls. Two panels below compare two approaches. Top-down memoization adds a cache so each distinct n is computed once, but keeps the recursion stack. Bottom-up tabulation fills the same table left to right with no recursion, shown as the climbing-stairs table where n = 1 through 5 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
images.caption: Top-down keeps the recursion stack; bottom-up fills the table in a loop.

options.text: Top-down computes only the subproblems it actually reaches; tabulation may fill cells that are never used.
Top-down can build a deep call stack and overflow it; tabulation uses a loop and avoids that.
Tabulation makes it easy to shrink memory by discarding old rows of the table.
Top-down is always more memory-efficient than tabulation.
Tabulation changes the time-complexity class compared with memoization for the same recurrence.

questions.explanation: Top-down only visits the subproblems the recursion actually needs, which helps when most states are never reached, but deep recursion can overflow the call stack. Tabulation runs as a loop, so there's no stack to overflow, and its fixed fill order makes it easy to keep only the last few rows. The false claims: for the *same recurrence*, tabulation and memoization have the *same* time complexity and differ only in constants, stack use, and which cells get computed. And top-down isn't always more memory-efficient, since it carries both the call stack and the cache.

questions.title: You climb a staircase 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to climb **5** stairs?
questions.description: Look for the overlapping subproblems: `ways(n)` reuses `ways(n-1)` and `ways(n-2)`.

images.alt: The full call tree for a naive recursive fib(5): fifteen nodes over five levels, branching into fib(4) and fib(3) and down to fib(1) and fib(0) leaves. Six nodes compute their value for the first time; the other nine are shaded as repeats of work done elsewhere in the tree. A side note says fib(40) takes over 300 million calls. Two panels below compare two approaches. Top-down memoization adds a cache so each distinct n is computed once, but keeps the recursion stack. Bottom-up tabulation fills the same table left to right with no recursion, shown as the climbing-stairs table where n = 1 through 5 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
images.caption: The bottom-up table: `ways(1)` through `ways(5)` are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

questions.explanation: Let `ways(n)` be the number of ways to reach step `n`. The last move is either 1 step (from `n-1`) or 2 steps (from `n-2`), so `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)`, the Fibonacci recurrence. Counting up: `ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, ways(3)=3, ways(4)=5, ways(5)=` **8**. Naive recursion recomputes `ways(3)`, `ways(2)`, and so on many times. Memoization or a bottom-up table makes it O(*n*).

questions.title: What does the **Levenshtein (edit) distance** between two strings count?

images.alt: The Levenshtein dynamic-programming grid for kitten against sitting. Seven rows are labeled with the empty string, then k, i, t, t, e, n; eight columns with the empty string, then s, i, t, t, i, n, g. The first row and column count up from zero, and the bottom-right cell holds 3. Its three neighbors are highlighted: 3 above-left, 4 above, 2 to the left. A legend gives the rule for filling a cell: up plus one is a deletion, left plus one an insertion, diagonal plus one a substitution, diagonal plus zero when the letters match, and you take the smallest. A footer traces kitten to sitten to sittin to sitting and notes that the grid has (n+1) by (m+1) cells, so filling it takes O(n·m) time.
images.caption: The edit-distance grid for `kitten` and `sitting`.

options.text: The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to turn one string into the other.
The number of characters the two strings have in common.
The number of positions at which the two strings differ, for equal-length strings only.
The length of their longest common substring.

questions.explanation: Levenshtein distance is the *minimum* number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions, or substitutions) needed to turn one string into the other. It powers "did you mean…?" suggestions, which look for dictionary words a few edits away. The option about "positions at which the two strings differ" describes Hamming distance. Hamming counts only substitutions and needs strings of equal length, so it can't handle the insertions and deletions that real typos produce.

questions.title: What does computing Levenshtein distance with the classic DP grid cost, for strings of length *n* and *m*?

images.alt: The Levenshtein dynamic-programming grid for kitten against sitting. Seven rows are labeled with the empty string, then k, i, t, t, e, n; eight columns with the empty string, then s, i, t, t, i, n, g. The first row and column count up from zero, and the bottom-right cell holds 3. Its three neighbors are highlighted: 3 above-left, 4 above, 2 to the left. A legend gives the rule for filling a cell: up plus one is a deletion, left plus one an insertion, diagonal plus one a substitution, diagonal plus zero when the letters match, and you take the smallest. A footer traces kitten to sitten to sittin to sitting and notes that the grid has (n+1) by (m+1) cells, so filling it takes O(n·m) time.
images.caption: Each cell comes from its top, left, and diagonal neighbors.

options.text: O(*n*·*m*) time to fill an (*n*+1)×(*m*+1) grid; space can be reduced to O(min(*n*, *m*)).
O(*n* + *m*) time and O(1) space.
O(*n* log *m*) time using binary search.
O(2^*n*) time, because edit distance is inherently exponential.

questions.explanation: The dynamic-programming solution fills a grid where cell `(i, j)` holds the edit distance between the first `i` characters of one string and the first `j` of the other. Each cell comes from its top, left, and diagonal neighbors in O(1), so the grid costs O(*n*·*m*). Each row depends only on the row before it, so you can keep just two rows (or one, carefully) and cut space to O(min(*n*, *m*)). It's not exponential: the DP table is exactly what stops the naive recursion from blowing up.

questions.title: In an fzf-style fuzzy finder, why does typing `"fb"` match `"FooBar"`?

options.text: Fuzzy matching treats the query as a **subsequence**: `f`, then `b`, appear in order, though not necessarily next to each other.
It computes a Levenshtein distance of 0 between `"fb"` and `"FooBar"`.
It treats `"fb"` as a prefix, and `"FooBar"` starts with `"fb"`.
It matches only because both strings contain the letter `b`.

questions.explanation: A fuzzy finder treats the query as a *subsequence*. The typed characters must appear in the candidate in the same order, with any gaps between them. In `"FooBar"` (lowercased to `"foobar"`), `f` is at index 0 and `b` at index 3, so `"fb"` matches. Prefix matching is stricter: the candidate would have to literally start with `"fb"`. (Prefix search is what a trie speeds up.)

questions.title: Why can naive fuzzy search over a large list be slow, around O(*n*·*m*) work per keystroke?

options.text: It checks each of *n* candidates and walks up to *m* characters in each one to test and score the match.
It re-sorts the whole list on every keystroke in O(*n*²).
It computes a cryptographic hash of every candidate string.
It re-downloads the candidate list from the server for each character typed.

questions.explanation: To match one candidate of length *m*, you walk through it looking for each query character in turn, which costs up to O(*m*). Across *n* candidates that's O(*n*·*m*), on *every keystroke*. With thousands of candidates, that's enough to drop frames. Real finders debounce input, cap the number of candidates, precompute lowercased strings, and skip non-matches early. Libraries such as fuzzysort rely heavily on these optimizations.

questions.title: Good autocomplete ranks matches instead of just filtering them. For the query `"cap"`, which match should usually rank **highest**?

options.text: A contiguous prefix like `"cap"` in `"caption"`, ahead of a scattered subsequence `c…a…p` in `"crispApple"`.
The longest candidate string, regardless of where the matched letters fall.
Whichever candidate happens to appear last in the source array.
Any match with the most letters in common, ignoring their order and position.

questions.explanation: Filtering asks *whether* a candidate matches; ranking asks *how well*. Practical scorers reward matches that are contiguous (the letters run together), that start at a word boundary or camelCase hump, and above all that form a *prefix* of the candidate. So `"cap"` at the start of `"caption"` beats the same letters scattered through `"crispApple"`. Length, position in the source array, and letter overlap that ignores order are poor signals of relevance.

questions.title: Which statements about edit distance and fuzzy matching are true?

options.text: With unit costs, edit distance is symmetric: `distance(a, b) === distance(b, a)`.
A "did you mean…?" spell-suggester ranks dictionary words by small edit distance to the typed word.
Subsequence (fuzzy) matching is more permissive than prefix matching.
The edit distance between two strings can exceed the length of the longer string.
Fuzzy finders require the query to be a contiguous substring of the candidate.

questions.explanation: When insertions, deletions, and substitutions each cost 1, swapping the two strings just swaps the insertions and deletions, so the distance is symmetric. Spell suggesters show dictionary words within a small edit distance of what you typed. Subsequence (fuzzy) matching is strictly looser than prefix matching. The two false claims: edit distance can never exceed the length of the longer string, because you can always substitute every character of the shorter one and insert the rest. And fuzzy finders allow *gaps* between matched characters; contiguous matches score higher, but they aren't required.

questions.title: If fuzzy matching is a case-insensitive **subsequence** test, which queries match `"FooBar"`?

options.text: `"oba"`
`"far"`
`"bar"`

questions.explanation: Lowercase the candidate to `"foobar"` (f0 o1 o2 b3 a4 r5) and check whether each query's letters appear left to right: `"fb"` → f0, b3 ✓; `"oba"` → o1, b3, a4 ✓; `"far"` → f0, a4, r5 ✓; `"bar"` → b3, a4, r5 ✓. `"rb"` fails: `r` is the last character (index 5), so there's no `b` after it. Order is what separates fuzzy matching from "contains all these letters".

questions.title: Which of these are real properties of practical fuzzy finders such as fzf and VS Code's Quick Open?

options.text: Matched characters must appear in the order they were typed.
Matches at word boundaries or camelCase humps are scored higher.
Contiguous runs of matched characters score higher than scattered ones.
The query must equal the candidate's full length exactly.
Letters may be matched out of order as long as all of them are present.

questions.explanation: Real finders require *order* (subsequence matching), then *rank* the matches. Matches at word starts or camelCase boundaries, and contiguous runs of matched letters, score higher because they usually reflect what you meant. The two false statements describe things finders avoid: they don't require the query to be as long as the candidate, and they don't allow out-of-order matches, which would let almost any query match almost anything.

questions.title: What is the Levenshtein distance between `"kitten"` and `"sitting"`?

images.alt: The Levenshtein dynamic-programming grid for kitten against sitting. Seven rows are labeled with the empty string, then k, i, t, t, e, n; eight columns with the empty string, then s, i, t, t, i, n, g. The first row and column count up from zero, and the bottom-right cell holds 3. Its three neighbors are highlighted: 3 above-left, 4 above, 2 to the left. A legend gives the rule for filling a cell: up plus one is a deletion, left plus one an insertion, diagonal plus one a substitution, diagonal plus zero when the letters match, and you take the smallest. A footer traces kitten to sitten to sittin to sitting and notes that the grid has (n+1) by (m+1) cells, so filling it takes O(n·m) time.
images.caption: The bottom-right cell holds the answer.

questions.explanation: This is the textbook example. Three edits turn one string into the other: `kitten` → `sitten` (substitute k→s) → `sittin` (substitute e→i) → `sitting` (insert g). No shorter sequence exists, so the distance is **3**. It mixes two substitutions and an insertion, and Hamming distance can't express insertions. That's why edit distance is the right model for typos.

questions.title: What is the Levenshtein distance between `"flaw"` and `"lawn"`?
questions.explanation: Two edits are enough: `flaw` → `law` (delete the leading `f`) → `lawn` (add `n` at the end), so the distance is **2**. The shared `"law"` makes 1 look plausible, but lining the strings up takes *both* a deletion and an insertion. When your intuition and the DP grid disagree, trust the grid.

questions.title: When flex items grow to fill a row, how does the browser share out the leftover space?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Greedy line breaking next to Knuth–Plass. Flexbox makes the same kind of decision without lookahead.

options.text: Greedily and proportionally: free space is split by each item's `flex-grow` ratio, with no search over alternatives.
By backtracking through every possible split and keeping the best one.
By sorting the items and giving all the free space to the largest.
Randomly, which is why the layout differs between reloads.

questions.explanation: Flexbox measures the free space on the main axis and splits it among the items in proportion to their `flex-grow` values: an item with `flex-grow: 2` gets twice the share of one with `flex-grow: 1`. Shrinking works the same way through `flex-shrink`, weighted by each item's base size. If an item hits its minimum or maximum size, the browser freezes it and shares what's left among the others. It never searches or backtracks, and nothing is random. It's a direct, deterministic calculation.
questions.references: [MDN: flex-grow](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/flex-grow) · [MDN: Controlling ratios of flex items along the main axis](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_flexible_box_layout/Controlling_ratios_of_flex_items_along_the_main_axis)

questions.title: How does a browser's **default** line-breaking algorithm decide where to wrap a paragraph?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Greedy first-fit never revisits a break, so it can strand a short last line.

options.text: Greedily: it fits as many words as it can on the current line, breaks, and moves on, one line at a time with no lookahead.
Optimally: it minimizes the raggedness of the whole paragraph before drawing any line.
By backtracking across all paragraphs to balance the page.
By sorting the words on each line from shortest to longest.

questions.explanation: The default line breaker is *greedy first-fit*: fill the line until the next word would overflow, break, and repeat. It's fast and takes a single pass, but it never reconsiders an earlier break, so it can leave a ragged right edge or a lonely short last line. The optimal alternative, which weighs the whole paragraph at once, is the Knuth–Plass algorithm, and browsers don't use it by default for body text. Greedy wrapping is good enough and cheap to compute.

questions.title: TeX's **Knuth–Plass** algorithm wraps paragraphs more evenly than greedy wrapping. Which technique does it use?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Knuth–Plass weighs all the break points together and avoids the stranded last line.

options.text: Dynamic programming: it minimizes the *total* "badness" across the whole paragraph, not one line at a time.
A greedy single pass, identical to the browser default.
Binary search over candidate font sizes.
A precomputed hash map of every possible line width.

questions.explanation: Knuth–Plass treats line breaking as one optimization over the whole paragraph. It gives each possible line a "badness" score (how stretched or cramped its spaces are), adds penalties for things like hyphenation, and then uses *dynamic programming* over the candidate break points to find the set of breaks with the lowest total badness. It will accept a slightly worse line if that makes the paragraph better overall, which avoids the loose, uneven lines greedy wrapping can produce. The cost is more computation.

questions.title: What does `text-wrap: pretty` actually do in Chrome today?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Chrome's `text-wrap: pretty` reworks only the final lines, not the whole paragraph.

options.text: It reworks the last few lines to avoid orphans and short final lines, which improves on greedy wrapping without optimizing the whole paragraph.
It runs complete Knuth–Plass optimization across the entire paragraph in every browser.
It justifies text by stretching the spaces, like `text-align: justify`.
It disables wrapping entirely and lets the text overflow its container.

questions.explanation: The CSS spec lets each browser choose the algorithm, and Chrome's version is deliberately limited. It looks at the *last* lines of a paragraph to prevent orphans and very short final lines, adjusting hyphenation if needed. That improves on greedy wrapping, but it doesn't re-optimize the whole paragraph the way Knuth–Plass does, and other engines behave differently. Its sibling, `text-wrap: balance`, evens out line lengths in short blocks such as headings.

questions.title: When matching a selector like `.menu li a` against an element, in which direction does a CSS engine check the parts, and why?

images.alt: Two panels. The left panel matches the selector .menu li a against one element: a nested chain of a div with class menu, a ul, an li, and an a, annotated right to left. Step 1 asks whether the element is an a, step 2 looks for an li ancestor, and step 3 for a .menu ancestor. A note says almost every element fails step 1 in one comparison, so the ancestor walk never starts. The right panel runs the regex caret open-paren a-plus close-paren plus dollar against four a's and an exclamation mark, and shows all eight ways to split the four a's between the inner and outer plus. A note says n a's give 2 to the power n minus 1 splits, and the trailing exclamation mark makes the match fail, so the engine tries every one: 524,288 attempts for twenty a's. Two footers separate what is backtracking (regex alternatives, selector ancestor walks, Sudoku, and N-queens) from what is not (a hash-map lookup, and flexbox dividing free space in one pass).
images.caption: Most elements fail step 1, so the ancestor walk never starts.

options.text: Right to left: it starts with the element itself (the `a`), then checks ancestors, so most non-matches fail after one cheap step.
Left to right, mirroring how the selector reads to a human.
In both directions at once, then it intersects the two result sets.
In order of specificity, trying the highest-specificity part first.

questions.explanation: Browsers check the *rightmost* part of the selector (the "key selector") against the element first, then walk up the DOM **right to left** to check the ancestor conditions. The reason is pruning. The engine is testing one specific element, and most elements fail the cheap first check (`is this an <a>?`), so it never has to look at ancestors. Going left to right would mean searching the descendants of every `.menu` for an element that one comparison could have ruled out.

questions.title: Why can a regex like `/^(a+)+$/` freeze the main thread on an input such as `"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!"`?

images.alt: Two panels. The left panel matches the selector .menu li a against one element: a nested chain of a div with class menu, a ul, an li, and an a, annotated right to left. Step 1 asks whether the element is an a, step 2 looks for an li ancestor, and step 3 for a .menu ancestor. A note says almost every element fails step 1 in one comparison, so the ancestor walk never starts. The right panel runs the regex caret open-paren a-plus close-paren plus dollar against four a's and an exclamation mark, and shows all eight ways to split the four a's between the inner and outer plus. A note says n a's give 2 to the power n minus 1 splits, and the trailing exclamation mark makes the match fail, so the engine tries every one: 524,288 attempts for twenty a's. Two footers separate what is backtracking (regex alternatives, selector ancestor walks, Sudoku, and N-queens) from what is not (a hash-map lookup, and flexbox dividing free space in one pass).
images.caption: Each extra `a` doubles the number of splits the engine has to try.

options.text: **Catastrophic backtracking**: nested quantifiers give exponentially many ways to split the input, and the engine tries them all before it can report failure.
The regex allocates one DOM node per `"a"`, exhausting memory.
JavaScript regexes compile to threads, and each `"a"` spawns a new one.
The `$` anchor forces a network round-trip to validate the string.

questions.explanation: Backtracking regex engines, the default in JavaScript and most languages, try alternative ways to match. With nested quantifiers like `(a+)+`, the run of `a`s can be split between the inner and outer `+` in exponentially many ways. If the string matches, the engine stops early. Here the trailing `"!"` makes the match *fail*, so the engine tries every split before giving up. That's roughly O(2^*n*) work, and it freezes the thread. This is a ReDoS risk. The fix is to rewrite the pattern without the ambiguous nesting; here, `/^a+$/` matches exactly the same strings.

questions.title: What characterizes a **backtracking** algorithm?

images.alt: Two panels. The left panel matches the selector .menu li a against one element: a nested chain of a div with class menu, a ul, an li, and an a, annotated right to left. Step 1 asks whether the element is an a, step 2 looks for an li ancestor, and step 3 for a .menu ancestor. A note says almost every element fails step 1 in one comparison, so the ancestor walk never starts. The right panel runs the regex caret open-paren a-plus close-paren plus dollar against four a's and an exclamation mark, and shows all eight ways to split the four a's between the inner and outer plus. A note says n a's give 2 to the power n minus 1 splits, and the trailing exclamation mark makes the match fail, so the engine tries every one: 524,288 attempts for twenty a's. Two footers separate what is backtracking (regex alternatives, selector ancestor walks, Sudoku, and N-queens) from what is not (a hash-map lookup, and flexbox dividing free space in one pass).
images.caption: Regex and selector matching both back up and try another path when one fails.

options.text: It builds a candidate step by step, abandons a partial solution as soon as it can't be completed, and goes back to try a different choice.
It always reaches the global optimum in a single greedy pass.
It caches subproblem results to avoid recomputation.
It divides the input in half at every step.

questions.explanation: Backtracking is systematic trial and error. You extend a partial solution one choice at a time, and as soon as a constraint is broken, you *undo* that choice (backtrack) and try the next option. That prunes whole branches that can't lead to a valid result. It's how Sudoku and N-queens solvers, regex alternation, and CSS selector ancestor checks work. The wrong options describe other approaches: greedy (commit in one pass), memoization and DP (caching), and divide-and-conquer or binary search (halving).

questions.title: Which statements about **greedy** behavior in CSS layout are true?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Greedy wrapping next to Knuth–Plass. Flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.

options.text: Flexbox shares out free space in proportion to `flex-grow`, without trying alternatives.
The default text line-breaker is greedy: it commits each line without reconsidering earlier breaks.
CSS Grid auto-placement fills cells in order, dropping each item into the next free slot.
Greedy algorithms always produce the globally optimal layout.
`flex-shrink` is resolved by backtracking over every possible item size.

questions.explanation: Layout is full of greedy decisions: flex grow and shrink distribution, the default line breaker, and Grid auto-placement, which walks the grid and puts each auto-placed item in the next free cell. The false claims get the limitation and the mechanism wrong. Greedy methods are fast but **not** guaranteed to find the best overall result (that's why Knuth–Plass exists for line breaking), and `flex-shrink` is a direct proportional calculation, not a backtracking search.

questions.title: Which of these involve **backtracking**?

images.alt: Two panels. The left panel matches the selector .menu li a against one element: a nested chain of a div with class menu, a ul, an li, and an a, annotated right to left. Step 1 asks whether the element is an a, step 2 looks for an li ancestor, and step 3 for a .menu ancestor. A note says almost every element fails step 1 in one comparison, so the ancestor walk never starts. The right panel runs the regex caret open-paren a-plus close-paren plus dollar against four a's and an exclamation mark, and shows all eight ways to split the four a's between the inner and outer plus. A note says n a's give 2 to the power n minus 1 splits, and the trailing exclamation mark makes the match fail, so the engine tries every one: 524,288 attempts for twenty a's. Two footers separate what is backtracking (regex alternatives, selector ancestor walks, Sudoku, and N-queens) from what is not (a hash-map lookup, and flexbox dividing free space in one pass).
images.caption: The footers sort examples into backtracking and not backtracking.

options.text: A regex engine retrying alternative matches when a branch fails.
A CSS selector engine walking up ancestors and abandoning a candidate that does not match.
Solving Sudoku or placing N queens by trying a value and undoing it on a conflict.
Looking up a value in a hash map by its key.
Distributing flex free space in proportion to `flex-grow`.

questions.explanation: Backtracking means trying a choice and *backing out* when it fails. Regex alternation and quantifiers retry other matches, selector matching gives up on an element once an ancestor check fails, and puzzles like Sudoku and N-queens place a value, then undo it on a conflict. The other two aren't backtracking: a hash-map lookup goes straight to its slot with nothing to undo, and flex distribution is a direct greedy calculation.

questions.title: Which statements about line breaking and text wrapping on the web are true?

images.alt: The same ten-word paragraph wrapped two ways in the same column, with words drawn as bars against a dashed right margin. The greedy first-fit version ends its five lines at 156, 156, 161, 237, and 95 pixels: the fourth line crams in three words and the fifth holds just one. The Knuth–Plass version ends at 156, 156, 161, 156, and 176, with no stranded last line. Notes explain that greedy fills each line until the next word would overflow and never revisits a break, while Knuth–Plass scores the badness of each candidate line and runs dynamic programming over all break points. A footer says that text-wrap pretty in Chrome reworks only the final lines, that text-wrap balance evens out short blocks such as headings, and that flexbox and Grid auto-placement are greedy too.
images.caption: Greedy wrapping can strand a short last line; Knuth–Plass avoids it.

options.text: Greedy wrapping is fast and on by default; whole-paragraph optimization (Knuth–Plass) is slower but more even.
`text-wrap: balance` aims to even out line lengths in short blocks such as headings.
`text-wrap: pretty` in Chrome focuses on the final lines to reduce orphans rather than re-optimizing the whole paragraph.
Browsers have always used Knuth–Plass by default for body text.
Optimal line breaking is impossible to compute, so no system does it.

questions.explanation: Here's the accurate picture. The default breaker is greedy: fast, one line at a time. Knuth–Plass optimizes the whole paragraph with dynamic programming, which is more even but slower. `text-wrap: balance` targets short multi-line blocks like headings, and Chrome's `text-wrap: pretty` currently polishes the last lines to avoid orphans instead of re-flowing everything. The two false claims are easy to check: browsers have used greedy wrapping, not Knuth–Plass, and optimal line breaking is clearly computable, since TeX has done it since the early 1980s.
